answer:
HYPOTHESIS: The variable is SES (Socioeconomic Status). In the baseline model of BA degree completion that includes only social background factors (SES, family size), the effect of SES is strongly positive and highly significant (coefficient 0.3636). When race and academic characteristics (standardized test ability / ASVAB composite score and related academic resources) are added to the model, the SES effect collapses to -0.2293 and loses statistical significance. This indicates that the apparent positive association between family socioeconomic status and bachelor's degree completion is explained away by racial differences and, especially, by academic ability/achievement: once race and academic performance are held constant, socioeconomic status no longer has a significant net effect (its point estimate even reverses sign), suggesting that the SES gradient in BA attainment operates largely through academic resources rather than as a direct effect.

Evidence from my own replication on the supplied data (8,773 rows, no missing values, 2.69% BA completion rate, White n=5337 / Black n=2113 / Hispanic n=1323, Female n=4437 / Male n=4336):
- SES is the ONLY predictor showing the reported pattern. In the baseline model (SES + family size + sex), SES is positive and significant in every specification; when effect-coded race and the ASVAB composite are added, SES becomes insignificant at the 5% level in a probit (0.3641 -> 0.0981, p=0.055) and flips to negative and insignificant in a linear probability model (+0.0141, p<0.001 -> -0.0032, p=0.22).
- The baseline magnitude 0.3636 is reproduced almost exactly by a probit model on the raw SES scale (0.3641; difference 0.0005), identifying the reported scale as probit-index (log-odds-like) coefficients rather than marginal effects or LPM probabilities.
- No alternative variable matches: family size remains strongly significant and negative in every model (-0.247 -> -0.196, p<0.001), and the academic variables (ASVAB, class percentile) are themselves significant in the augmented model, so none of them exhibits the flip.
- Caveat on the exact augmented value: across the full spec grid (probit/logit/LPM x raw/z x dummy/effect race coding x ASVAB-only/ASVAB+percentile), no specification reproduced -0.2293 exactly; the closest insignificant SES estimates were +0.098 (probit, p=0.055) and -0.003 (LPM, p=0.22). The exact -0.2293 likely reflects the source analysis's fuller sample/specification - notably the dataset documentation mentions curriculum as an academic resource, but no curriculum column exists in the staged CSV, so the academic-characteristics control set could not be fully replicated.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8773 rows, no missing values; BA completion rate 2.69%). Estimated baseline models of BA degree completion on social background (SES, family size, sex) and augmented models adding race and academic characteristics (ASVAB composite, class percentile) across a grid: probit/logit/linear probability model x raw/standardized predictors x effect/dummy race coding x ASVAB-only vs ASVAB+percentile. Recorded each predictor's coefficient and p-value in each specification. SES is the only variable whose effect loses significance when race and academic characteristics are added; its baseline probit coefficient (0.3641) reproduces the reported 0.3636 almost exactly, identifying the probit-index scale. In the LPM the SES effect reverses to negative and insignificant, consistent with the sign reversal in the reported augmented coefficient. Family size remains strongly significant and negative in all specifications, ruling it out. The exact augmented value -0.2293 was not exactly reproducible from the staged subset (closest: +0.098 p=0.055 probit; -0.003 p=0.22 LPM), likely because the source analysis used a curriculum measure that is not present in the staged CSV. Curriculum check confirmed: no curriculum-like column exists in the data.
